The bandit is initialized with a prior that assumes all user segments have equal expected CTR across arms. After 2 weeks, engagement analysts notice the bandit performs well for mobile users but poorly for desktop users — desktop CTR has declined 8% since deployment versus baseline. They suspect the prior is misspecified for desktop users. A data scientist proposes three interventions: (1) re-initialize the desktop user segment with a new prior fit from pre-bandit desktop data, (2) add desktop-specific features to the ridge regression, and (3) run a separate bandit for desktop users. Rank the interventions from most to least effective at addressing the core problem.
options: 3, 2, 1 — A separate desktop bandit is best because it eliminates the shared parameter problem; adding features is second because it gives the model more signal; prior re-initialization is least effective because the model will simply re-learn the same incorrect patterns

2, 1, 3 — Adding contextual features is best because it allows the single model to learn desktop-specific patterns; prior re-initialization is second because it gives the desktop segment a better starting point; a separate bandit is least effective because it discards cross-segment information

1, 3, 2 — Prior re-initialization is best because it directly addresses the misspecification; a separate bandit is second because it allows clean learning; adding features is least effective because more features increase variance without fixing the prior

2, 3, 1 — Adding contextual features is best because it most directly addresses the root cause (the model lacks desktop-specific signal); a separate bandit is second because it avoids cross-segment contamination; prior re-initialization is least effective because it is a temporary fix that does not change the model's ability to learn desktop patterns
explanation: The core problem is that the bandit model lacks sufficient desktop-specific signal to learn appropriate arm preferences for that segment. A uniform prior and a model that does not adequately distinguish desktop behavior from mobile behavior will systematically underperform for any segment that behaves differently from the population average. Adding contextual features (intervention 2) most directly addresses this: if the ridge regression model can learn that desktop users respond differently to content types or presentation formats, it will adapt its arm preferences for desktop users as data accumulates. This is the most scalable and enduring fix. A separate bandit (intervention 3) is second: it completely eliminates cross-segment contamination and allows the desktop bandit to develop its own arm distribution independently, at the cost of lost cross-segment information that may have been useful. Prior re-initialization (intervention 1) is the least durable: while it gives the desktop segment a better starting point, the same ridge regression model structure that failed to learn desktop patterns will continue to do so unless the model itself (not just the prior) is improved. Option A undervalues feature addition and overvalues model separation. Option B correctly prioritizes feature addition but places prior re-initialization second over a separate bandit — this is debatable but defensible.
hints: When a model performs poorly on a specific subgroup, consider whether the issue is in how the model is initialized (prior) or in whether the model architecture can represent the subgroup's behavior at all.
Rank interventions by whether they fix the root cause (model expressiveness), address a symptom temporarily (prior), or avoid the problem by isolation (separate model).

title: Multi-Armed Bandit vs Fixed A/B: Long Horizon Decision
description: A subscription SaaS company is testing three pricing page variants (A, B, C) against a control. The experiment will run for 8 weeks across 40,000 new visitors per week. Historical data shows pricing experiments at this company have a high variance in outcomes — some variants have large positive effects (>10%), others are neutral or slightly negative. The head of growth wants to use a Thompson sampling bandit to minimize revenue lost during the experiment. The head of analytics argues that for this particular scenario, a fixed 4-arm A/B test with equal allocation is preferable. What is the strongest argument supporting the analytics head's position?
options: A bandit cannot handle 4 arms; Thompson sampling is only valid for binary (2-arm) experiments, making the fixed A/B test the only valid design
The fixed A/B test produces a cleaner causal estimate with well-calibrated confidence intervals, which are required for the post-experiment business review

With high variance in historical outcomes, the bandit may concentrate traffic on a variant that happens to perform well early due to noise rather than true superiority, especially with 40,000 visitors per week and 8 weeks of data — the fixed design ensures the exploration phase is long enough to overcome early noise and identify the true winner more reliably
Fixed A/B tests always provide higher statistical power than bandits for the same total sample size, making the analytics head's position universally correct
explanation: The analytics head's strongest argument is about noise-driven early allocation in a high-variance environment. Thompson sampling concentrates traffic toward the arm with the highest posterior probability of being best. In a high-variance outcome environment, early observations can be noisy — a variant that happens to perform well in the first week due to random fluctuation will accumulate more traffic, reinforcing its dominance in the posterior even if the true effect is no better than control. With 40,000 visitors per week, there is substantial weekly traffic, but 8 weeks is a relatively short window to overcome high-variance outcomes through posterior updating alone. A fixed equal-allocation A/B test forces continued exploration of all arms throughout the experiment, ensuring each arm accumulates enough observations to average out noise before a final decision. The analytics head is also correct that the bandit's regret-reduction advantage is greatest when the true winner has a substantially larger effect and can be identified quickly — which the high-variance historical pattern suggests may not be reliably the case here. Option A is false — Thompson sampling handles multiple arms natively. Option B is a secondary consideration about decision process, not a statistical argument. Option D is false — bandits can have higher or lower power depending on the scenario; 'always higher' is incorrect.
hints: Thompson sampling allocates more traffic to the arm that looks best early — in a high-variance environment, what does 'looking best early' tell you about true superiority?
Think about the conditions under which a bandit's regret advantage over fixed allocation is largest — and whether those conditions are present when historical effect sizes are highly variable.

title: SUTVA Violation: Social Network Cascade
description: A social network runs an experiment on a new 'group post reaction' feature — users in the treatment group can react to group posts with an expanded set of emoji. The experiment randomizes 20% of users into treatment. After 4 weeks, the treatment group shows 15% higher group post engagement. However, a network analyst points out that group posts are viewed by all members of a group regardless of their experimental assignment. A treatment user's reaction (using an expanded emoji) is visible to control users in the same group, potentially stimulating their engagement as well. After adjusting for this interference via a network-aware model, the estimated effect drops to 9%. An engineer proposes a simple fix: randomize groups rather than individual users. A scientist pushes back on this proposal. What is the scientist's strongest objection?
options: Group-level randomization is technically infeasible on large social networks because groups have millions of members and cannot be cleanly partitioned

Group-level randomization would eliminate the interference problem but dramatically increases the variance of the treatment effect estimate: groups are highly heterogeneous in size, activity, and user composition, so group-level random assignment introduces much higher variance in the measured treatment and control outcomes compared to individual randomization

Group-level randomization introduces a new problem: users belong to multiple groups, so a user could be in a treatment group for one community and a control group for another, making the individual-level treatment condition ambiguous and reintroducing interference
Group-level randomization is only valid when groups are of equal size; unequal group sizes require a different clustering approach
explanation: The scientist's strongest objection is that group-level randomization does not solve the interference problem if users belong to multiple groups — which is the typical structure on social platforms. A user who is in a treatment group (where expanded emoji reactions are available) will also be a member of control groups (where the feature is unavailable). When that user reacts to a post in their treatment group with an expanded emoji, other control-group users who are also in that same treatment group see it. Conversely, the treatment user sees only standard reactions in their control groups. The user-level treatment condition becomes undefined, and interference across group boundaries persists. Additionally, the treatment user's behavior in control groups is contaminated by their experience in treatment groups. Option A is empirically untrue — many platforms randomize at the group or community level. Option B is a real concern (higher variance with group randomization due to heterogeneous group sizes), but it is a statistical efficiency tradeoff, not a fundamental validity objection. Option D is incorrect — unequal cluster sizes in cluster-randomized experiments are handled via appropriate analysis weights; they do not invalidate the design.
hints: When users belong to multiple groups, and randomization assigns groups (not users) to treatment conditions, what happens to an individual user who is simultaneously in a treatment group and a control group?
Think about whether the proposed solution actually eliminates the interference channel or whether it moves the problem to a different boundary.

title: Network Interference: Bipartite Graph Randomization
description: An online tutoring marketplace runs an experiment to test an AI-powered question hint system for tutors. Tutors use the system to generate hints for students. The platform has 5,000 tutors and 50,000 students; each student works with 1–3 tutors. The team randomizes tutors into treatment (hint system available) and control (no hint system). After 6 weeks, treatment tutors' students show 8% higher assessment scores. A researcher argues that the estimate is still biased by interference. Some students work with both a treatment tutor and a control tutor: insights a student gains from a treatment tutor's hints may improve their performance with their control tutor as well. The interference flows through students, not directly between tutors. This is described as 'bipartite graph interference.' What is the correct direction of bias in the tutor-level treatment effect estimate?
options: The estimate is biased upward: treatment tutors get credit for score improvements that are partly caused by their students' learning gains from other treatment tutors, inflating the apparent effectiveness of the hint system

The estimate is biased downward: students shared between treatment and control tutors carry learning spillovers from treatment tutors into their sessions with control tutors, raising control tutor student scores and compressing the treatment-control gap

The estimate is unbiased: bipartite graph interference only affects student-level randomization, not tutor-level randomization, because the interference flows through students who are not the unit of randomization

The estimate could be biased in either direction depending on whether treatment tutor spillovers dominate or control group contamination dominates; the direction cannot be determined without knowing the fraction of students who are shared
explanation: The bias is downward, and the direction can be reasoned precisely. Students who work with both a treatment tutor and a control tutor benefit from the hint system (via their treatment tutor) and carry that learning into sessions with their control tutor. The control tutor's student scores are therefore elevated — not by the hint system applied by the control tutor, but by the treatment spillover through the shared student. This elevates the control group's outcome metric, compressing the gap between treatment and control. The treatment effect estimate (treatment tutor student scores minus control tutor student scores) is therefore smaller than the true effect. Option A describes the opposite direction: credit flowing to treatment tutors from other treatment tutors is not the described mechanism; the mechanism is student-mediated spillover into the control arm. Option C is incorrect: bipartite interference affects any randomization where the interference pathway runs through shared units (students in this case) — tutor-level randomization does not eliminate this. Option D correctly notes that the fraction of shared students matters for the magnitude, but the direction of bias (downward) is deterministic given the described mechanism.
hints: Think about what happens to the control group's outcome when some control-group subjects have also been exposed to the treatment through a different connection — does that raise or lower the control group average?
When spillovers from the treatment arm contaminate the control arm's outcomes, does that make the treatment-control gap look bigger or smaller than the true effect?

title: Long-Term Holdout: Novelty Decay vs True Effect
description: A consumer app launches a major redesign affecting the home screen. A 4% holdout group (600,000 users) is kept on the old design for 12 months to measure long-term effects. At 30 days, treated users show 18% higher daily active use. At 90 days, the gap is 11%. At 180 days, the gap is 7%. At 360 days, the gap is 4%. The product team interprets this as novelty decay: early excitement with the new design fades over time. A researcher challenges this interpretation, offering an alternative explanation. What is the most credible alternative explanation for the declining gap, and what data would distinguish between the two interpretations?
options: The alternative explanation is that control (holdout) users have been learning about the new design from treatment users via social communication, and are partially adapting their habits to the new design despite not having access to it; the distinguishing data would be social graph adjacency between holdout and treatment users

The alternative explanation is that the old design's performance is degrading over 12 months as the product team focuses engineering resources on improving the new design, raising the control group's defect rate and suppressing their engagement; the distinguishing data would be server-side error rates and load times for the control (old design) code path

The alternative explanation is that the holdout group is self-selecting into lower engagement over time because more engaged users are more likely to request access to the new design (or be granted access through CS tickets), leaving behind a holdout population skewed toward lower-engagement users; the distinguishing data would be composition analysis of holdout users over time (activity levels, tenure) compared to an enrolled holdout at each time point

The alternative explanation is that the metrics being measured (daily active use) are lagging indicators of long-term habit formation, and a 12-month gap of 4% represents the true sustained benefit while early higher gaps are noise; distinguishing data would be session-level behavioral depth metrics rather than top-line DAU
explanation: The most credible alternative explanation is holdout attrition bias through composition drift. Over 12 months, the most engaged and motivated users in the holdout group are most likely to notice they have a different experience, complain, seek the new design via customer support tickets, or use workarounds (e.g., switching devices). If these high-engagement users are preferentially leaving the holdout group — either by being moved to treatment or by churning from the platform entirely — the holdout population becomes increasingly composed of lower-engagement users over time. A holdout group shrinking in average engagement looks like the treatment-control gap is narrowing, when in reality the holdout baseline is deteriorating due to composition change. This is distinct from novelty decay (which would show treated user engagement declining back toward baseline rather than the control group declining toward treatment). The distinguishing data is composition analysis: if the holdout group's baseline engagement distribution is shifting toward lower values over 12 months while a freshly enrolled cohort shows stable distributions, composition drift is the likely explanation. Option A (social spillover) is possible but weak — the mechanism for significant behavioral adaptation without access to the new design is unclear. Option B (old design degradation) would show up in system metrics and is testable but less likely as a smooth, monotonic trend over 12 months. Option D mischaracterizes the pattern as noise and doesn't provide a mechanism for the decline.
hints: When a holdout group is maintained for 12 months, consider whether the composition of that holdout group might be changing over time — which users are most likely to leave the holdout, and what does that do to the group average?
Novelty decay means treatment users' behavior is returning toward a baseline — holdout composition drift means the control baseline itself is changing. What data would reveal each mechanism?

title: Holdout Group Cannibalization: Multi-Feature Attribution
description: A fintech app has maintained a 2% global holdout group for 18 months while the product team shipped 23 separate features. The holdout group now has 14% lower monthly active use than the treatment population. The team wants to attribute this 14% gap to individual features to prioritize which ones to invest in further. A data scientist proposes using the holdout group's single 14% gap to decompose feature contributions by correlating the timing of each feature launch with step changes in the holdout-vs-treatment gap over the 18 months. An experimentation researcher argues this approach has a fundamental flaw. What is it?
options: The 2% holdout size is too small for reliable attribution analysis; individual feature contributions would have confidence intervals too wide to be actionable

The holdout group has been accumulating treatment-control divergence for 18 months — the features interact with each other over time, and users in the treatment group have been adapting their habits to the combined set of features for 18 months; attributing step changes in the gap to individual features ignores these interaction effects and the compounding of behavioral changes

Correlating step changes in the gap with launch timing conflates causation and correlation: a feature may launch during a period when the gap would have widened anyway due to seasonal effects or other confounders

The holdout group should have been replenished with new users every 6 months to remain representative; after 18 months, the holdout population is too different from the treatment population for any attribution analysis to be valid
explanation: The fundamental flaw is that the 14% gap reflects the combined, compounding effect of 23 features over 18 months — not the sum of 23 independent additive contributions. Users in the treatment group have been building habits, discovering features, and adapting their workflows in a holistic experience of all 23 features simultaneously. Features interact: a new search feature may become more valuable after a filtering feature is added; a notification feature's effect may depend on whether users have the mobile widget feature. Over 18 months, these interactions compound in ways that cannot be recovered by looking at step changes in the aggregate gap at each launch date. The step-change approach assumes that each feature's contribution is the discrete jump in the gap at its launch date and does not persist or interact with subsequent features — this is an unrealistic model of user behavior. Additionally, users in both groups are changing over time independently (tenure effects, seasonality), making causal attribution of step changes to specific features unreliable. Option A is a precision concern, not the fundamental flaw. Option C is a valid secondary concern about confounding but is not the core structural problem. Option D introduces a 'holdout replenishment' norm that is not standard and does not address the core attribution problem.
hints: When 23 features have been shipped to a single treatment group over 18 months, and users have been adapting to all of them simultaneously, can the cumulative gap be decomposed by feature using a step-change approach? Think about what assumption that requires.
Features shipped sequentially to a single population do not have independent effects — consider how user behavior adapts to a combined product experience over a long time horizon.

title: Combined Variance Reduction: CUPED and Stratification Interaction
description: A data scientist at a marketplace is designing an experiment on seller fee negotiation outcomes. She plans to use both stratified randomization (by seller GMV quintile) and a CUPED adjustment (using each seller's pre-experiment GMV as the covariate). She notes that the CUPED covariate (pre-experiment GMV) is strongly correlated with the stratification variable (GMV quintile, r ≈ 0.88). Her manager proposes dropping the CUPED adjustment since stratification already handles the GMV variation, and adding a second covariate — seller account age — to CUPED instead. The data scientist disagrees. What is the most rigorous argument for her position?
options: The data scientist is right: CUPED should never be dropped even if the stratification variable is highly correlated, because CUPED additionally removes within-stratum variance that stratification does not address; dropping CUPED and replacing it with account age as the sole covariate would capture less variance unless account age has a higher within-stratum correlation with the outcome than pre-experiment GMV

The manager is right: when the stratification variable and CUPED covariate are highly correlated (r = 0.88), CUPED adds negligible variance reduction beyond stratification, and using a second independent covariate (account age) would provide more incremental variance reduction

The data scientist is right: it is always better to include more covariates in CUPED regardless of their correlation with the stratification variable, since additional covariates can only reduce or maintain variance and never increase it

The manager is right: double-adjusting for the same variance source (GMV) via both stratification and CUPED leads to over-controlling, which increases the standard error relative to using stratification alone
explanation: The data scientist's argument is correct and precise. Stratified randomization reduces between-stratum variance by ensuring each stratum has equal treatment/control proportions. However, within each stratum, there is still substantial variation in pre-experiment GMV — the stratification by quintile creates homogeneous groups in terms of rank but not in terms of continuous GMV values. CUPED uses the continuous pre-experiment GMV as a covariate, which removes variance at a finer granularity than the quintile strata. The two methods therefore address related but not identical variance: stratification removes between-stratum variance, CUPED additionally removes within-stratum variance that is correlated with the covariate. Even with r = 0.88 between the continuous covariate and the quintile variable, there is meaningful within-stratum variance remaining for CUPED to explain. The manager's proposal to replace pre-experiment GMV with account age in CUPED would only be better if account age has a higher within-stratum correlation with the outcome than pre-experiment GMV — which is unlikely since GMV is typically the strongest predictor of its own future values. Option B is approximately correct about the marginal gain from CUPED being reduced by stratification, but wrong to conclude it should be dropped. Option C is too absolute — covariates with negligible correlation with the outcome add variance through estimation rather than removing it. Option D incorrectly diagnoses 'over-controlling' as a risk in this context.
hints: Stratified randomization removes variance between groups defined by the stratum — but within each stratum, there is still variation. What can CUPED address that stratification cannot?
When the stratification variable and CUPED covariate are correlated but not identical (r = 0.88, not 1.0), think about whether CUPED is entirely redundant or still captures additional variance.

title: Interference Modeling: Equilibrium vs Local Treatment Effects
description: A food delivery platform tests a new driver incentive structure. Individual drivers are randomized: 40% receive new bonuses (treatment), 60% receive standard compensation (control). After 6 weeks, treatment drivers complete 12% more deliveries per day than control drivers. The platform wants to use this estimate to project the steady-state impact of rolling out the new incentive to all drivers. A senior economist argues that the 12% estimate cannot be directly used for this projection. The platform has a fixed pool of orders — there is no evidence the new incentive generates additional consumer demand. What is the economist's argument, and is she correct?
options: The economist is wrong: the 12% lift is a valid direct estimate of the productivity gain from the new incentive structure, and rolling out to all drivers will yield a 12% platform-wide delivery increase

The economist is right: in the experiment, treatment drivers' additional completions come partly by capturing orders that would have been completed by control drivers; at full rollout with no control group, the total order pool is fixed, so the same 12% individual lift cannot materialize at the platform level — the equilibrium effect will be smaller and depends on the supply-demand response

The economist is right but only because the incentive increases driver costs; if the cost increase reduces driver supply at full rollout, the net platform-wide completions would fall below the current level

The economist is wrong: because individual driver productivity is measured at the individual level, equilibrium effects only matter for consumer-facing metrics like delivery time, not for driver-level completion rates
explanation: The economist is correct, and her argument is about the distinction between a partial equilibrium (experiment) estimate and a general equilibrium (full rollout) effect. In the experiment, 40% of drivers receive the new incentive and 60% do not. The treated drivers are more motivated to complete deliveries — they may accept orders faster, decline fewer requests, and work longer hours. In a marketplace with a fixed order pool, these additional completions by treated drivers come partly at the expense of control drivers, who receive fewer order opportunities because treated drivers are absorbing them first. The control group's completion rate is therefore artificially suppressed by competition from treated drivers, and the 12% gap is partly a within-experiment redistribution rather than a true productivity gain. At full rollout — when all drivers receive the new incentive — there are no control drivers to displace. The incremental completions cannot come from the same redistribution mechanism. The true platform-level effect depends on whether the incentive actually reduces driver idle time and churn (genuine productivity) versus simply redirecting orders among drivers. Option A ignores the supply-demand equilibrium structure of the marketplace. Option C raises a valid but different concern about cost and supply; this could be relevant but is not the economist's stated argument about the fixed order pool. Option D incorrectly claims equilibrium effects are only relevant for consumer-facing metrics — they are relevant for any metric measured in a shared resource environment.
hints: When treatment and control units compete for the same finite resource, what happens to the control group's access to that resource during the experiment — and what does that imply about the size of the measured effect?

Think about what changes when the experiment ends and the treatment is applied to everyone: which part of the treatment-control gap was driven by redistribution rather than genuine productivity, and does that part persist at full rollout?

title: Long-Run Holdout Group Decay: When the Counterfactual Diverges from Current Users
scenario_context: A major consumer tech platform maintains a permanent 5% holdout group excluded from all product feature launches. After two years of continuous feature deployment, the holdout group's weekly active usage is 23% lower than the treatment group. Product leadership declares a 23% cumulative lift from all features deployed over the two-year period. The data science team raises a validity concern about this attribution.
description: What is the primary validity concern with attributing the 23% usage gap to the cumulative effect of deployed features?
options: A two-year holdout group has experienced a fundamentally different product: no UX improvements, no recommendation updates, no performance work — users who found the unimproved product inadequate may have churned or severely reduced usage, leaving a survivor population that is self-selected and no longer representative of what current treatment users would look like without treatment; the 23% gap conflates the causal effect of features with compositional divergence and differential attrition between the two groups over time

The 23% estimate is directionally correct but should be time-discounted: features deployed in month 1 had 24 months to compound their effect while features deployed in month 23 had only 1 month; applying a time-weighted discount to each feature's individual contribution would reduce the headline 23% to a smaller but internally consistent cumulative lift estimate

The measurement is valid because the holdout group was randomly assigned two years ago; random assignment at baseline is sufficient for valid causal inference at any subsequent measurement horizon, regardless of how divergent the two groups' product experiences have become over the two-year period

The 23% gap underestimates the true feature impact: holdout users who churn do so because the inferior product fails to retain them, removing the least-engaged users and biasing the surviving holdout toward users who derive less incremental value from features; the true average treatment effect on the full user population is therefore larger than 23%
explanation:
Option A is correct. A holdout group's validity as a counterfactual rests on the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA): holdout users' behavior must represent what treatment users would have done without treatment. Over two years, the holdout group experienced a product that fell progressively further behind the treatment product in quality. Users who needed improvements to stay engaged may have churned or reduced usage to accommodate the degraded experience. At the two-year mark, the holdout population is self-selected: survivors are those who tolerated an increasingly outdated product, a fundamentally different population from the average treatment user. Comparing treatment users (who received all features and retained engagement accordingly) against surviving holdout users confounds the causal feature effect with this compositional divergence and differential attrition.

Option B introduces time-value discounting, which is not a correction for compositional validity. The usage gap is a point-in-time measurement — current weekly active usage. Discounting individual feature contributions does not address the self-selection bias in the holdout population's composition at the measurement date.

Option C is wrong. Random assignment at baseline is necessary but not sufficient for valid long-run causal inference when the two groups have experienced radically different conditions and differential attrition for an extended period. Random assignment eliminates baseline confounding; it does not insulate against the compositional drift that occurs when the two groups experience different products and therefore exhibit different retention behavior over two years.

Option D's argument is plausible in structure but wrong in conclusion here. Whether heavy users benefit more or less from incremental features depends on feature type. More critically, Option D does not address the compositional validity concern — it accepts the gap as a valid causal estimate and merely debates its magnitude. The data science team's concern is about the validity of the comparison, not its direction.
hints: After two years without any product improvements, how likely is the holdout group's current composition and engagement level to represent what treatment users would look like without treatment? What has happened to holdout users who found the unimproved product inadequate?

Random assignment at the start of a holdout period ensures the groups are initially comparable. Does it guarantee they remain comparable after two years of experiencing different product quality, different recommendation quality, and different retention pressures?

title: Switchback Experiment Analysis: Temporal Autocorrelation Inflates the Test Statistic
code_snippet:
# Ride-share platform: 7-day switchback experiment
# Treatment/control alternates by day; ~200K active users/day
# Metric: average ride completions per user

periods = pd.DataFrame({
    'day':             [1,    2,    3,    4,    5,    6,    7],
    'treatment':       [1,    0,    1,    0,    1,    0,    1],
    'avg_completions': [4.82, 4.71, 4.85, 4.69, 4.79, 4.73, 4.83]
})

treat = periods[periods.treatment == 1]['avg_completions']
ctrl  = periods[periods.treatment == 0]['avg_completions']

from scipy.stats import ttest_ind
t_stat, p_val = ttest_ind(treat, ctrl)
print(f't={t_stat:.2f}, p={p_val:.3f}')  # Output: t=5.17, p=0.035
description: The t-test declares the experiment significant at α = 0.05 using 4 treatment periods and 3 control periods. A colleague argues this analysis is fundamentally flawed. What is the primary error, and what is the correct analytical approach?
options: The t-test treats 4 treatment days and 3 control days as 7 independent observations, but daily rideshare completions are serially autocorrelated — the same commuting patterns, weather, and events make adjacent days correlated regardless of treatment assignment; this autocorrelation means the effective sample size is much smaller than 7 and the standard error is underestimated, inflating the t-statistic and producing a false-positive; the correct approach uses cluster-robust or Newey-West standard errors that account for within-week temporal dependence, or a mixed-effects model with a random effect for time block

The fatal flaw is unequal group sizes: 4 treatment periods vs 3 control periods violates the equal-n requirement for a two-sample t-test; reassigning day 7 to control to achieve a balanced 3-vs-3 design eliminates the bias from the extra treatment observation

avg_completions is a ratio metric; all ratio statistics require delta method variance correction before a t-test is valid; ttest_ind significantly underestimates the variance for ratio metrics, inflating the t-statistic by approximately √n for a dataset of this size

A switchback experiment with only 7 periods cannot satisfy the Central Limit Theorem requirement for normality of period-level means; a minimum of 30 periods is required before the t-test approximation is valid; the result should be discarded and the experiment extended to at least 30 alternating periods
explanation:
Option A is correct. The standard independent-samples t-test assumes each observation is drawn independently from its population. In a time-series switchback experiment, daily averages are not independent — the same commuters travel on Monday and Tuesday, weekly seasonality (weekday vs weekend patterns) persists across adjacent days, and external shocks (weather, events) simultaneously affect consecutive days. Positive autocorrelation means observations share information: the effective number of independent data points is much smaller than 7. The t-test's standard error formula assumes independence and therefore underestimates the true standard error, inflating the t-statistic. The numerical pattern here (treatment days: 4.82, 4.85, 4.79, 4.83; control days: 4.71, 4.69, 4.73) is highly consistent within each group — a signature of correlated measurements, not independent sampling. The correct approach: cluster the standard errors at the day level (cluster-robust SE), apply Newey-West HAC correction, or use a mixed-effects model with a random intercept for time that absorbs the serial correlation before computing the treatment coefficient.

Option B is wrong. Unequal group sizes in a two-sample t-test do not bias the estimate — ttest_ind handles unequal n correctly by default using Welch's t-test. Reassigning an observation to achieve balance would reduce information. Unequal n is not a validity issue.

Option C applies to a different scenario. avg_completions here is the mean of a count metric computed over 200K users per day — not a ratio with a highly variable denominator. With 200K users per day, the CLT applies strongly to the daily mean, and the variance of the mean is well-estimated without delta method correction. The dominant error is autocorrelation, not ratio variance.

Option D is incorrect. There is no universal 30-period minimum for switchback experiments. The CLT approximation applies when observations are independent and the distribution of the test statistic converges — with positive autocorrelation, the problem is the violated independence assumption, not the period count. Even 100 periods of positively autocorrelated data would produce inflated t-statistics under a standard t-test.
hints: The t-test treats each day as an independent observation. In a rideshare market, is Tuesday's average ride count independent of Monday's? What shared factors create correlation between adjacent days in a time-series?

Positive autocorrelation between observations means consecutive measurements carry overlapping information — the effective sample size is smaller than the nominal count. How does overestimating the effective sample size affect the computed standard error and the resulting p-value?
